video_title: Replit CEO Amjad Masad on What Young People Should Learn in the AI Era
gist: Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Gagan, founder of a new two-year Silicon Valley 'academy' that Replit backs, argue that college's prescriptive, grade-driven model fits the AI era poorly. They favor curiosity-led, project-based learning in which AI lets every student build a custom path. Most of the conversation is about education and culture; the market-relevant signals are Masad's claims that AI-driven ML research ('vibe research') is where agentic coding was in 2024 and is becoming a new Replit business line, that agents will make 'self-driving companies' possible, and that pre-idea VC checks to students amount to predatory premature optimization.

themes.theme: Agentic coding to auto ML research

insights.claim: Amjad Masad says ML research is now where coding was in 2024 when Replit Agent launched, before the term 'vibe coding' existed: AI can now do machine-learning work itself (recursive self-improvement / 'auto research'), which he thinks will change ML the way agents changed coding.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: AI-automated model training and ML research looks like the next category after vibe coding. Watch for agentic ML tooling to become its own product segment.
insights.quote: I realized that AI is actually, you know, capable of doing ML.

insights.claim: Replit is building a product that lets anyone become a machine learning researcher, so that any business owner with data can train their own model for a specific problem. Amjad Masad describes it as a new Replit business line that came out of a personal chess project.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: Replit plans to expand from app building into custom model training for SMBs and non-experts, which puts it into competition with ML platform vendors.
insights.quote: I'm working on something on Replit to to to bring that to to the world like where anyone can become a machine learning researcher

insights.claim: Amjad Masad found that general-purpose LLMs like ChatGPT play chess poorly and hallucinate illegal moves despite rising ARC-AGI scores. He trained his own chess LLM, his first model, to explore how models are trained.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: The gaps frontier models still have in specific domains are an opening for fine-tuned, task-specific models, which is the market Replit's ML product targets.

insights.claim: Amjad Masad says that in 2025 he was 'canceled' for saying people should no longer learn to code. A year later, engineers who opposed him tell him they no longer read code and just prompt.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: Professional engineers adopted prompt-driven coding within about a year, a signal of fast demand for AI coding tools and of pressure on traditional coding education.
insights.quote: Now, the same people that were like went against me, they're like, "Oh, I don't read code anymore. I just like prompted by code."

insights.claim: Amjad Masad argues that past org-structure experiments such as Holacracy at Medium and GitHub's no-managers model failed because of a technology problem. AI agents can now act as the invisible bureaucratic glue so people have real autonomy, and he is moving Replit toward a 'self-driving company' that eventually runs itself.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: If agents absorb coordination work, companies need less middle management and back office. That is a demand driver for enterprise agent platforms.
insights.quote: we call this idea of like a self-driving company eventually like the company will like run itself

insights.claim: Gagan, the academy founder, uses Replit, Claude and ChatGPT to speed up his own work (he built his pitch deck in Replit). He says organizations will change much faster than people expect, and those not natively fluent with AI will struggle to adapt.
insights.speaker: Gagan (academy founder)
insights.so_what: Founders are using AI tools for non-coding work, such as decks, which widens the addressable market beyond developers.
insights.quote: It's going to change a lot faster than you think.

insights.claim: Amjad Masad calls it predatory that VCs give Stanford students about $1 million before they have an idea, and compares it to music-industry contracts that lock in young artists. He says SAFEs (from YC and Paul Graham) help, but students still end up committed to ideas they are not passionate about, with a cap table from day one.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: Pre-idea student funding is being criticized by prominent founders. Expect adverse selection and higher failure rates in envy-driven teen startups.
insights.quote: I've heard that VCs go to Stanford students and they give them like a million dollars, not even 50K.

insights.claim: Amjad Masad applies the programming idea that 'premature optimization is the root of all evil' to young founders: many start companies out of envy of friends who became unicorns, on ideas they don't care about. He says he actively tried not to start Replit and only did so when it grew into a startup on its own.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: A founder-quality screen: back founders whose ideas pull them in on their own momentum, not ones funding-driven by peer envy.
insights.quote: I think a lot of starting startups is premature optimization.

insights.claim: Gagan argues only a very small number of teenagers should raise money. Temporary grants are fine, and a two-year, pressure-free exploration period backed by Silicon Valley resources suits most young builders better than either four-year college or a funded startup.
insights.speaker: Gagan (academy founder)
insights.so_what: This is a new alternative-education and talent-pipeline model that sits between college and accelerators.

insights.claim: Gagan says AI makes customized, project-based curricula practical at scale: students can learn a language like Python by building something they care about, with no custom syllabus needed. He points to Alpha School (Joe Liemandt, captioned 'Joe Lehman') as the model of teaching through students' interests.
insights.speaker: Gagan (academy founder)
insights.so_what: AI-native schools like Alpha School and project-based programs are positioned against traditional curricula, which is relevant to edtech investing.
insights.quote: now is the moment when it's completely reverted and it's not just impossible it's actually impossible to imagine why you wouldn't do that

insights.claim: The academy that Gagan is launching, with Replit's support, has no grades, no tests and no graduation requirement. It offers two years of exploration, and students may intern at Replit and potentially be funded by it.
insights.speaker: Gagan (academy founder)
insights.so_what: Replit is building an early-talent pipeline, a sign that AI companies are creating their own alternatives to college for hiring.
insights.quote: We don't have grades. We don't have tests.

insights.claim: Amjad Masad argues college's traditional promise no longer holds: you can do very well in college and still be unemployed with huge debt. He says young people are most useful as 'heretics' who question deeply held beliefs, including Silicon Valley's own monoculture.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: Masad sees the ROI of traditional degrees weakening, which is a headwind for incumbent higher-ed and student lending.
insights.quote: You can do really well in college and you can still be unemployed with a huge debt.

insights.claim: Amjad Masad proposes routing teen hackers, many of whom learn programming and hacking on Roblox, into sandboxed bounty programs and cybersecurity jobs, including at the NSA, instead of prison. He says he raised the sandbox idea with Roblox's founder and CEO.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: Roblox is effectively a pipeline for cybersecurity talent at a time of shortage, an angle on training and recruiting platforms.
insights.quote: We need cyber security talent right now.

themes.theme: High-trust Valley culture as an edge

insights.claim: Gagan says a verbal $50,000 commitment in nonprofit fundraising converts to cash only 20-50% of the time, versus about 75-100% in Silicon Valley. That trust lets founders keep building before the money arrives, which compounds progress.
insights.speaker: Gagan (academy founder)
insights.so_what: A high-trust capital ecosystem means faster execution, one reason Bay Area startups move quicker than outside ecosystems.

insights.claim: Amjad Masad says Silicon Valley is no longer a renegade outsider but part of the establishment, so the 'autistic genius' persona no longer pays off (he cites Sequoia's deleted SBF post). He criticized a Dwarkesh blog post, which Bernie Sanders read, for giving non-experts the wrong lessons about the technology.
insights.speaker: Amjad Masad (Replit CEO)
insights.so_what: AI industry messaging now reaches policymakers directly, so careless communication raises regulatory and political risk for the sector.
insights.quote: I think Silicon Valley is no longer this sort of renegade thing.
